'''José Félix Mendieta Villarroel''' (born 15 November 1958) is a Bolivian politician and trade unionist who served as a member of the [[Chamber of Deputies (Bolivia)|Chamber of Deputies]] from [[Cochabamba Department|Cochabamba]], representing circumscription 28 from 2010 to 2015.

Though educated in [[pedagogy]], Mendieta spent most of his career in commercial driving, climbing the ranks of the sector's trade unions to eventually become general secretary of the Sacaba Mixed Motor Transport Union. Though traditionally conservative, under the leadership of figures like Mendieta, many of the country's drivers' unions were reoriented towards the left.

Starting in the early 2000s, the driving sector's alliance with the [[Movement for Socialism]] opened spaces for many of its representatives to attain elective office. Such was the case with Mendieta, who, from 2005 to 2009, served on [[Sacaba Municipality|Sacaba]]'s municipal council before later being elected to represent the area's drivers' unions in the Chamber of Deputies.

{{TOC limit|2}}

== Early life and political career ==

=== Early life and education ===
José Mendieta was born on 15 November 1958 in [[Sacaba]], [[Cochabamba Department|Cochabamba]], to Profacio Mendieta and Florencia Villarroel.{{sfn|Vargas|Villavicencio|2014|p=102}} Mendieta was raised in a household of [[Lower middle class|modest means]];{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|p=368}} his father worked as a commercial driver while his mother was a local merchant. He completed his primary studies at the Germán Busch School, later attending the José Nicolas Maldonado School before seeking [[higher education]] in [[pedagogy]], graduating from the Enrique Finot Normal School.{{sfn|Gonzales Salas|2013|p=92}} He briefly taught mathematics at an institution in [[Warnes, Bolivia|Warnes]] but retired after just two years due to the financial constraints and low income received from practicing the profession.{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|p=368}}

=== Career and trade unionism ===
Unable to continue teaching, Mendieta returned to Sacaba, where he dedicated himself to commercial driving. In the ensuing years, he became affiliated with the city's drivers' unions, spending nearly a decade in leadership roles in the Sacaba Mixed Motor Transport Union, including holding office as the organization's general secretary for six years.{{sfn|Gonzales Salas|2013|p=92}}

Under Mendieta's leadership, the organized drivers continued to push for their historical demands, such as the lowering of excessive [[Toll road|tolls]] or the expansion of fuel access. However, they were also oriented in favor of broader social issues, with Mendieta supporting [[Mass mobilization|mobilizations]] against the [[Water privatization in Bolivia|privatization of water]] and in favor of [[resource nationalism]].{{sfn|Vargas|Villavicencio|2014|p=102}} His tenure represented a broader trend of realignment on the part of the country's transportation sector—long unique for its more conservative orientation in comparison to other unions—towards left-wing political positions.{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|pp=17; 256}}

The shift in disposition among the drivers' unions coincided with the rising primacy of the nascent [[Movement for Socialism]] (MAS-IPSP), with both groups steadily coalescing into a broader alliance.{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|p=17}} Already in 2004, Mendieta was invited by the MAS to run for a seat on the Sacaba Municipal Council, a position he won.{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|pp=368–369}} His tenure as a municipal councillor focused on guaranteeing the water supply in Sacaba,{{sfn|Gonzales Salas|2013|p=92}} a region that continued to suffer debilitating shortages in the wake of the [[Cochabamba water conflict]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Forero |first=Juan |author-link=Juan Forero |date=2005-12-14 |title=Bolivia Regrets IMF Experiment |language=en |work=[[The New York Times]] |location=Cochabamba |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/12/14/business/worldbusiness/bolivia-regrets-imf-experiment.html |url-status=live |access-date=2022-10-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220516201610/https://www.nytimes.com/2005/12/14/business/worldbusiness/bolivia-regrets-imf-experiment.html |archive-date=2022-05-16}}</ref>

== Chamber of Deputies ==

=== Election ===
{{Further|2009 Bolivian general election}}
The alliance between the MAS and the drivers' unions solidified from [[2005 Bolivian general election|2005]] on and translated into the nomination of at least one union representative per department.{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|pp=199; 211}} Mendieta's prominence as a local transport leader led Sacaba's drivers' union to select him as their representative in parliament.{{sfnm|1a1=Vargas|1a2=Villavicencio|1y=2014|1p=102|2a1=Romero Ballivián|2y=2018|2p=369}} Customarily, candidates chosen by the drivers' unions were registered on the MAS's [[electoral list]], but Mendieta's municipal experience led the party to run him in a [[single-member constituency]]. He won by an absolute majority in Cochabamba's circumscription 28, one of the MAS's primary bases of support.{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|p=369}}

=== Tenure ===
As was the case on the municipal council, Mendieta spent much of his tenure in the [[Chamber of Deputies (Bolivia)|Chamber of Deputies]] working to improve access to water in Cochabamba's underdeveloped regions, for which he spent most of his term heading the chamber's Natural and Hydric Resources and Water Committee.{{sfn|Vargas|Villavicencio|2014|p=102}} Mendieta's term as chair also saw significant developments in Bolivia's dispute with Chile regarding sovereignty over the [[Silala River]]. In late 2012, the committee, followed shortly thereafter by the Chamber of Deputies and the [[Chamber of Senators (Bolivia)|Senate]], passed a bill declaring the river's waters a strategic natural resource. "We are ratifying with this law our full right over these water resources," Mendieta stated, "we do not have to ask permission from anyone, not from Chile{{Nbsp}}... or any other country on the use of the Silala."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Quenallata |first=René |date=2012-11-24 |title=Aguas del Silala son recurso natural estratégico según ley |language=es |trans-title=Silala Waters Are a Strategic Natural Resource, Law Affirms |work=[[Opinión]] |publication-place=Cochabamba |url=https://www.opinion.com.bo/articulo/el-pais/%EF%BB%BFaguas-silala-son-recurso-natural-estrategico-ley/20121114213100438042.html |url-status=live |access-date=2023-01-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230102094225/https://www.opinion.com.bo/articulo/el-pais/%EF%BB%BFaguas-silala-son-recurso-natural-estrategico-ley/20121114213100438042.html |archive-date=2023-01-02}}</ref>

Nearing the conclusion of his mandate, Mendieta was not nominated for reelection,{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|p=369}} a common practice among the Movement for Socialism, which preferred to open up spaces for different representatives of allied sectors to enter parliament.{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|p=320}} Though Mendieta's political career ended there, Cochabamba's drivers' unions maintained their parliamentary presence through the elections of legislators such as Lucio Gómez.{{sfn|Romero Ballivián|2018|pp=256; 369}}
